title: Pocket reads: long-context jotter
content:
Quick pocket notes from papers / talks / demos this week — mostly for myself, messy. Goal: capture interesting heuristics for long-context inference and small experiments to try on Redwood infra.

1) High-level takeaways (very rough)
- Contextual compression seems practically useful: chunk & compress then re-expand in LM space (cf. 'compression-as-retrieval' idea). Big win when token budgets are tight.
- KV cache sparsity + prioritized retention beats FIFO for long sessions — prioritization heuristics based on token novelty and recency windows.
- Prefix stores + cheap sketches (bloom/LSH) to quickly check if a segment is likely relevant before decompressing. Good trade for Dedicated pools where cold fetch is costly.

2) Papers / demos I skimmed (notes to follow up):
- "Skim & Stitch: lightweight compression for long context" (workshop slide) — idea: build two-tier cache: compressed summaries (cheap) + hot full tokens. Measure recall at top-k retrieval.
- "Sparse-KV Retention" (ICML talk) — retention score = alpha*recency + beta*surprisal; tuned per user workload.
- ArXiv:2601.01234 — toy experiments on distillation-to-prefix; results promising for 8k->64k context scaling.

3) Small experiments to try on Redwood infra (priority order)
- A: Implement retention score simulator on small logs (chat dumps) — quick python sim, compare FIFO vs retention by recall@N for retrieval tasks. Metric: downstream generation perplexity + latency.
- B: Build a tiny prefix-store prototype (Redis + LSH index) that stores compressed chunk embeddings and a small sketch. Flow: query sketches -> candidate list -> decompress top candidates. Measure extra latency and hit rate.
- C: Quantize compressed representations (8-bit) and see how much it reduces memory bandwidth during fetch.

4) Practical constraints & thoughts for Redwood product fit
- Hosted API use cases: want minimal extra latency (prefetching important). For short interactive calls, heavy decompress not OK — need async prefetch + best-effort freshness.
- Dedicated: can trade off more memory for faster decompress on GPU. Could provide an "extended context" add-on where customers pay for prefix-store capacity (maybe priced per GB-month + egress).
- Private/VPC: ops team will want deterministic eviction policies and auditability — retention heuristics must be explainable.

5) Open questions / uncertainties
- How to evaluate perceived quality drop when compressing history vs explicit retrieval? Need human evals but start with automated proxies (PPL, task-specific F1).
- How big should chunks be? Too small -> many metadata entries; too big -> compression hurts retrieval. Adaptive chunking?
- Is there an efficient on-device decompress kernel we can reuse on GPU (vs CPU)? If not, decompression can create CPU->GPU bottleneck.

6) Quick action items (next 2 weeks)
- [ ] Owen: share sample chat logs (anonymized) from customer-sim set (due 2026-06-25).
- [ ] Me: write retention-score sim skeleton and run on two datasets by 2026-06-30.
- [ ] Maya: prototype simple LSH sketch for chunk filtering (POC by 2026-07-05).

7) Random heuristics to test (notes)
- Retention score: 0.6*recency_norm + 0.4*(1 - token_overlap_with_recent)^2
- Keep top-K chunks per conversation where K scales with conversation length^(0.7) — empirical knob.

8) Links & refs to read later
- workshop slides + video (saved in my Drive folder)
- arXiv:2601.01234 (see linked_artifacts)
- GH: reddit/context-compression-probe (synth data scripts)

Notes-to-self: keep these lightweight — the goal is a rapid iteration loop: simulate -> small POC -> cheap eval -> show SRE/console implications. If retention sim looks promising, schedule a 30-min sync with eng-serving-runtime to discuss implementation constraints (KV format, eviction hooks, traceability).

End of jotter (will clean later).
